questions.q: In the Caldwell & Finch Insurance case study, what two symptoms turned out to share one root cause?
options: Customers receiving duplicate renewal emails, and a customer-count metric that crept up without real growth
A server outage and a missed payroll deadline
A missing invoice and an incorrect tax calculation
A slow website and a failed software update
questions.explain: Both the duplicate-email complaints and the inflated customer count traced back to the same underlying cause: duplicate customer records in the merged unified view.

questions.q: Why does each of the three source systems (CRM, Policy Administration, Support Ticketing) create its own separate customer record?
options: Each system has its own trigger for first creating a record, and each uses a different identifier — CRM_ID, PolicyHolderID, or email address alone
Because all three systems are actually copies of the same database
Because company policy requires triplicate paperwork for every customer
Because the systems were all built by the same vendor using identical schemas
questions.explain: Each system creates a record under different circumstances (first sales contact, policy issuance, or first support ticket) and keys it differently, with no shared identifier.

questions.q: What specifically caused the same real customer to appear as multiple rows in the unified customer view?
options: The merge logic matched records by email address, and slightly different formatting of the same email caused mismatches
The unified view intentionally duplicates every customer for backup purposes
Customers were asked to register twice on purpose
The CRM system deleted all customer records every night
questions.explain: Formatting differences like J.Smith@email.com versus j.smith@email.com for the same person caused the matching logic to treat them as different customers.

questions.q: What did tracing upstream and downstream from the unified customer view reveal about impact?
options: It fed four separate consumers — marketing, a leadership metric, a churn calculation, and a compliance report — all affected the same way
It had no downstream consumers at all
Only the marketing team's campaign was affected
The unified view was not actually connected to any other system
questions.explain: The case study found four downstream consumers, all quietly wrong in the same direction because they all read from the same flawed merge.

questions.q: What was the lesson's description of the real, lasting fix, beyond the immediate email-formatting patch?
options: Designating the CRM's identifier as the authoritative source of record, requiring other systems to capture it, and documenting the cross-system lineage explicitly
Deleting the Support Ticketing system entirely
Switching all three systems to use random customer IDs
Removing the unified customer view and reverting to three separate reports
questions.explain: The structural fix was assigning a deliberate, authoritative matching key across all three systems, rather than continuing to rely on an informal email-based match.
